title: Remembrance
hookLine: poppies, silence, and prayers for all who died in war

lines: A RED FLOWER ON A COAT.
cards: A red paper flower, pinned to a coat. Then on a bus driver, a newsreader. In some countries, poppies like these bloom on coats each autumn, and then, on one morning, a whole street goes quiet.
Traffic stops. A shop falls silent mid-sale. At a stone memorial, someone reads a poem, and the crowd answers it with a few plain words: we will remember them.
Churches keep this day too, praying for all who died in war, soldiers and civilians, names known and names lost.

teach.b: The flower comes from an old war poem, In Flanders Fields, which sees poppies blowing between rows of crosses over the graves of the dead. The red poppy grew, so the usual account goes, out of that picture.
It isn't a Bible symbol. But the church already had words for this day. First, silence.

Ecclesiastes has a poem of times and seasons, and in the middle, in the King James words: "a time to keep silence, and a time to speak." At Remembrance, the silence comes first, before any speech or name. Second, love.
On the night before he died, Jesus told his friends: "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends." Some memorials carry that line, cut into stone.
Many Christians hear it first about Jesus himself, then about anyone who gave their life for someone else. Third, hope. Remembrance is not a celebration of war.
Isaiah saw a day when the nations "shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more."
Some churches read that line at Remembrance, and pray for the dead of every side. Christians disagree about war.
Some churches accept that a nation may fight to defend the weak; others refuse to bear arms at all, and keep this day with their whole weight on peace. Both can stand in the same silence.
For many Christians, that silence is a kind of prayer: holding the dead before God, and asking for fewer names to read next time.

how: In some countries, churches hold Remembrance services with poppies, a two-minute silence at a memorial, names of the dead read aloud, and prayers for peace and for all who died in war.

games.q: in Isaiah's vision, the nations come with swords and spears. what do they do with them?
o: hang them up in the temple as trophies.
beat them into plowshares and pruninghooks.
bury them where no one will find them.
games.why: they beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruninghooks: farm tools, for feeding people. and they learn war no more.

practice: Keep two minutes' silence, standing if you can, and bring to mind one person who died in a war: a face in an old family photo, a name on a memorial, someone from the news, or, if no name comes, the ones nobody remembers.
Don't fill the silence with thinking; let it be heavy. If you pray, hold them before God with Isaiah's hope, neither shall they learn war any more; if you don't, just stand with them.

wordCard.voice: Remembrance. Standing still together for all who died in war, with poppies, silence, and prayer for peace.
